text:
2. Searching with the GovInfo API

2.a. API Query
I used the assignment’s example query to search the Congressional Hearings collection:
collection:(CHRG) AND "Committee on Foreign Relations"
The search request used a page size of 100 and sorted results by publication date in descending order. I selected the first ten results for download.


2.b. Package Metadata and Pagination
For each package ID, I requested /packages/{packageId}/summary to retrieve the package metadata and available download links. The search response also included an offsetMark, which can be sent with another request to retrieve the next page of results. The process can continue until a response returns no results.

3. Downloading and Comparing the Documents

3.a. Downloading the Documents
I downloaded the ZIP files for the ten API search results and saved them in the files folder inside my working directory. I kept a download log containing each package ID, title, and download status. All ten documents in the log have the status Downloaded.


3.b. Comparing the Website and API Results
The website and API searches returned six of the same package IDs:

The two lists differed because the searches used different query fields and search methods. The website query specified the committee and chamber, while the API query searched for the phrase “Committee on Foreign Relations” within the CHRG collection. As a result, the API search could return a document that mentioned the phrase without being a hearing of that committee. For example, the API-only result CHRG-119shrg61202 is a hearing about illicit drug trafficking from the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.


3.c. Download Log
I kept the download log with the package IDs, titles, and download statuses. The log provides a record of which documents the API script attempted to download and whether each download succeeded.

title: Assignment 5
text:
4. Evaluating the Downloaded Documents

4.a. Using the Documents as Data
The PDFs are useful for reading and reviewing the hearings, but they are not immediately ready for analysis as data. To analyze them as a corpus, I would extract the text and create a table with one row per hearing and fields such as package ID, title, date, committee, participants, and extracted text.
I would then check and clean the extracted text. Page headers and footers, line breaks, tables, and speaker labels may need attention because they can affect searches and text analysis. I would also compare the extracted text with the original PDF to check for missing or incorrectly converted content.


4.b. Improving the Process
The ZIP package I inspected included the PDF as well as HTML and XML files, including MODS metadata. The metadata could be used to collect information such as titles and identifiers without opening each document. HTML or text files may also be easier to search and process than PDFs, so I would compare the available formats and choose the one best suited to the analysis.
I could also improve the search by applying committee and chamber fields to the API query, so that the API search more closely matches the website search. Keeping the query, package IDs, and download statuses in a log would make the process easier to review and reproduce.


4.c. What the API Provided
The API returned structured package metadata and download links, allowing me to search for and retrieve documents programmatically. It also supported paginated searches through the offsetMark, which can be used to request successive pages of results.

title: Assignment 3
text:
Uncertainty in the Estimates
I used the ACS MOEs to calculate approximate 90% confidence intervals for the two tracts with the highest estimated poverty rates. The values below are calculated from proportions and then expressed as percentages.

uncertainty_check <- top10 |>
  slice_head(n = 2) |>
  mutate(
    `Rate (%)` = 100 * pov_rate,
    `MOE (percentage points)` = 100 * pov_moe,
    `Lower bound (%)` = 100 * (pov_rate - pov_moe),
    `Upper bound (%)` = 100 * (pov_rate + pov_moe)) |>
  select(
    Tract = NAME,
    `Rate (%)`,
    `MOE (percentage points)`,
    `Lower bound (%)`,
    `Upper bound (%)`)

title: Assignment 3
text:
Methods
I used tidycensus to retrieve 2024 ACS 5-year estimates for census tracts in Dallas County, Texas. I mapped median gross rent (B25064_001). I calculated the poverty rate by dividing the number of people below the poverty level (B17001_002) by the population for whom poverty status is determined (B17001_001). I retained the margins of error for the estimates and used moe_prop() to calculate the MOE for the poverty rate. The table presents the 10 highest and 10 lowest estimated poverty rates, along with their estimates and MOEs. Tracts with large MOEs require caution when interpreting their rankings. In particular, the approximate 90% confidence intervals for the two highest estimates overlap, so their point-estimate ranking does not establish a difference in their underlying poverty rates. The ACS 5-year estimates summarize a five-year period, not conditions in 2024 alone.

In the KWIC examples, Biden recalled spending time with Xi in China, while reporters asked Trump what role Xi might play in the Russia–Ukraine war. Some matches came from editorial notes and name indexes, so the surrounding text helped identify who mentioned Xi and why.

The prominence of q, a marker for reporters’ questions, suggests that document format contributes to the difference. The analysis also counts words in passages unrelated to Xi, so the results describe the vocabulary of the selected documents as a whole.



The archived tweets show what users discussed around the November 2021 Biden–Xi summit. Twitter users wrote for online audiences, and the collected posts frequently mentioned Taiwan, tensions, and accounts such as @POTUS and @nytimes. The keyword and collection window shape whose posts and which topics appear in the sample, limiting what it can say about public opinion.
The presidential documents capture official remarks intended for audiences such as reporters and the public. They also include reporters’ questions and editorial material. Because the CPD search spans several years, it shows how Xi appeared in official records across different events. A direct comparison of online discussion and official messaging about the November 2021 summit would require narrowing the government documents to that event.

3. What is Wordfish?









Wordfish models word counts with a Poisson distribution. The expected count depends on a document effect, a word’s overall frequency, and how strongly the word is associated with the document’s position on a single estimated dimension. The dir argument fixes the direction of that scale because reversing the signs of both the document positions and the word associations yields the same fitted counts. I use the earliest and latest included addresses to orient the scale. In the fitted model, earlier addresses generally had lower scores and more recent addresses had higher scores. Democratic and Republican addresses overlapped across the scale. This pattern suggests that the dimension captures changes in inaugural language over time, although the plot alone cannot identify which changes drive the scores. To interpret what it measures, I would inspect the words associated with each end, read the speeches at the extremes, and check whether the positions track time, party, or another feature of the speeches.

Thirty-six Wikipedia entries did not exactly match a non-aggregate World Bank country name. For example, the sources may use different names, such as South Korea and Korea, Rep., or Turkey and Türkiye. Nineteen entries had an exact matching country name in the World Bank data but no 2024 value. Therefore, these 55 entries do not indicate that the reported values disagree; they could not be directly matched in this comparison.
The reference periods also differ. The World Bank values are annual observations for 2024, and the data retrieved here were last updated on October 8, 2026. Wikipedia’s reporting dates vary by country, and some are from 2025–2026. For example, Wikipedia reported approximately USD 253,767 million for the United States on August 22, 2025, while the World Bank’s 2024 value was approximately USD 910,037 million. For China, Wikipedia reported approximately USD 3,854,885 million on August 1, 2026, compared with approximately USD 3,456,025 million in the World Bank’s 2024 data.
The large difference for the United States may reflect not only the different reference periods but also different gold valuation methods. The World Bank says gold is valued at the year-end London price. In contrast, the U.S. Treasury’s international reserve position values gold at the statutory price of USD 42.2222 per ounce. Thus, gold valuation may be one contributor to the difference in the U.S. comparison.


3c. When is scraping the right tool?
Scraping is useful when no suitable API or bulk-download file provides the needed data and the website permits automated access. Requests should be sent at a reasonable pace, data should be cached, and the page structure and values should be checked for unexpected changes or errors.

title: Assignment 7
text:
This collection examines comments on 2026 US midterm election coverage by NBC News, CNN, and Al Jazeera English, representing a national network, cable news, and an international broadcaster. All requests were made on November 10. “Before” and “after” primarily identify video publication periods, not separate collection waves. This retrospective design cannot reconstruct what comment sections looked like before Election Day.
I searched “US midterm election” using relevance and view-count rankings, requesting 100 videos per ordering. The publication windows were September 1–October 27 and November 4–November 10. Both rankings returned 100 rows without duplicate video IDs, while reporting approximately one million available results. Only 24 videos overlapped before the election and 29 afterward. Before the election, Al Jazeera led relevance results with 16 videos, whereas CNN led view-count results with 38. These differences demonstrate that search rankings select different coverage rather than provide a random sample.
Channel uploads supplied an alternative route. An initial 200-video request per channel reached only November 6–7; expanded 6,000-video requests reached September 1 for all three. The broad title filter also captured foreign elections and a university faculty senate. Reviewing 20 retained and 20 excluded titles motivated a narrower filter. Generic program titles could still conceal relevant coverage. Ten candidates per channel and period were randomly drawn with seed 6302 and reviewed; the first three were selected before inspecting comment counts.
The resulting 18 videos yielded 2,708 unique comments, capped at 300 per video. All collection logs recorded success. CNN reached the cap on every selected video, producing 1,800 comments; Al Jazeera contributed 275 and NBC 633. Smaller sections matched their reported totals. For capped sections, the cap explains an observed shortfall; moderation, deletion, replies, and changing counts remain possible general sources of mismatch. Missing video IDs in some returned replies were repaired using the request’s video ID before joining metadata.
A comment section is therefore a sample of visible participation under these videos, conditional on access and moderation. People who watched without commenting are absent, and prolific authors can contribute several observations. Channel differences also combine topic selection with audience responses. Consequently, neither the raw counts nor the lexical comparisons identify a causal election effect. Comparing different videos before and after the election does not hold their subjects or audiences constant.
Participation and attention were uneven. The most active 10% of identified authors produced 22.7% of comments, while the top approximately 1% of comments received 43.8% of likes. Twenty-three repeated text groups contained 60 comments. These counts do not establish automated or coordinated behavior. NBC’s after-period videos had a 33.9% reply share, compared with CNN’s 2.2%, but selected topics and collection caps limit comparisons.
The quanteda unit was one comment. URLs and mentions were removed; emoji and non-English text were retained. Context reading distinguished party references, political support, procedural discussion, grievances, and uses of “democratic” unrelated to party identity. Required phrases were compounded alongside “vote blue” and “voter fraud.” Keyness emphasized celebration and Michigan in Al Jazeera comments and interview subjects in NBC comments. CNN’s leading Arabic features originated in only three comments, with 552 occurrences. Excluding those comments shifted the ranking toward laughter, Mississippi, and ridicule, demonstrating sensitivity to concentrated repetition.
LSD2015 classified 52.0% of Al Jazeera’s after-period comments as positive, versus 23.5% before. However, AI-assisted human coding of 40 randomly selected comments agreed with the dictionary on only 57.5%, below a 70% majority-class baseline in that sample. Sarcasm, political endorsements, abbreviations, mixed evaluations, and non-English text complicate interpretation. Zero or tied dictionary scores do not demonstrate emotional neutrality. These results describe lexical classifications, not validated changes in voter sentiment.
Assignment 6’s archived Biden–Xi tweets represent platform users selected by keywords and timing; their original collection cannot be repeated through the same access. Presidential documents mentioning Xi represent institutionally produced communication selected by publication practices and a query, supporting claims about government discourse. YouTube comments instead reflect self-selected participants under selected videos, shaped by audiences, moderation, ranking, and collection time. Public reads may be repeated, but exact results will change. None of these corpora alone represents public opinion. Retained code, manifests, and aggregates document the procedure while raw YouTube data must be deleted by December 10.

text:
2. Inspecting the Website Data

2.a. Date Range and Number of Observations
The downloaded file covers September 1, 2021, through September 1, 2026. The data are reported monthly, with 61 observations for each search term.


2.b. Reporting Interval
When the time window was set to the past five years, Google Trends reported the data at monthly intervals. After I changed the time window to the past 12 months and downloaded the data again, the reporting interval changed from monthly to weekly. The 12-month file covers September 14, 2025, through September 13, 2026, and contains 53 weekly observations for each search term.


2.c. Units and Normalization
The values are not raw search counts. They represent relative search interest normalized on a scale from 0 to 100. Google calculates each term’s search interest relative to all searches in the selected geography and time period and then rescales the results. A value of 100 represents the point at which relative search interest was highest within the query. A value of 0 does not necessarily mean that no searches occurred; it may indicate that relative interest was very low or that there was not enough data to report.


2.d. Removing a Search Term
After I removed Election from the query and downloaded the data again, the values for the remaining terms did not stay the same. Trump’s values changed in all 61 months, and its maximum increased from 39 to 100. Kamala Harris’s values changed in 29 of the 61 months, and its maximum increased from 8 to 19.
This happened because Google Trends normalizes and rescales the results within each individual query. Removing one term changes the comparison used to construct the 0–100 scale. Therefore, values obtained from differently specified queries are not directly comparable.

A Note on Search Terms
The time series for Harris and Kamala Harris were not identical. Although both terms showed sharp increases around major political events in 2024, search interest in Harris was generally higher. The word Harris can refer to a county, a supermarket chain, and many other people besides Kamala Harris.
This difference illustrates a problem of construct validity: the observable search term does not perfectly represent the theoretical concept that the researcher intends to measure. Using the broader term Harris introduces measurement error because searches about Kamala Harris are combined with unrelated searches. text:
4. Comparing the Two Collection Methods

4.a. Comparing the Time Series
The website and gtrendsR results differed in both their date ranges and reporting intervals. The website data covered September 1, 2021, through September 1, 2026, and contained 61 monthly observations for each search term. The R data covered September 12, 2021, through September 13, 2026, and contained 262 weekly observations for each term, for a total of 786 observations.
To make an approximate comparison, I aggregated the weekly R observations by calculating their monthly averages. For Trump, the R monthly average was lower than the website value in all 61 months. On average, the R values were 7.71 points lower. For Election, the R monthly average was lower in 60 of the 61 months and was 3.15 points lower on average.
Despite these differences in magnitude, the two sources showed very similar patterns over time. The correlation between the website and R series was 0.992 for Trump and 0.997 for Election. I could not directly compare the remaining series because the website query used Kamala Harris, whereas the R script used Harris. The differences between the two sources may reflect their different reporting intervals, search terms, sampling, and normalization procedures.


4.b. Evaluating the Two Methods

Reproducibility
With the website method, the researcher must manually record the query settings and retrieval time. If that information is missing, another researcher may not be able to reproduce the search. With gtrendsR, the search terms, geography, time window, category, and search type are written directly in the code, making the query easier to repeat.
However, Google Trends relies on sampled data, so running the same code again may not produce exactly the same values. To preserve the precise dataset used in an analysis, researchers should save the original CSV file and record its retrieval time in addition to saving the code.


Provenance
The gtrendsR method provides a clearer record of how the data were generated because the query settings remain in the code. By contrast, a CSV downloaded from the website may not preserve every setting selected by the user or the exact retrieval time, so those details must be recorded separately.
The R method does not automatically record the retrieval time either. Researchers should therefore include the date and time in a filename, code comment, or research log.


Scale
The website is manageable when only a few search terms are needed. If a researcher needed data for 50 terms, however, repeatedly entering query settings and downloading separate files would take considerable time and increase the risk of human error.
With gtrendsR, loops or functions can automate the collection and storage of data for many search terms and countries. This makes the R method more scalable. Nevertheless, Google Trends limits the number of terms in a single query and may restrict repeated requests, so a large collection task may need to divide the terms into smaller groups and pause between requests.


Fragility
Both methods can fail. With the website method, the Google Trends interface may change, or the researcher may accidentally select the wrong settings or download the wrong file. With the R method, gtrendsR relies on an unofficial connection to Google Trends. Changes to the Google service or website structure may therefore cause the code to stop working. Rate limits, internet problems, and package updates may also produce errors or unexpected results.
Researchers can identify these problems by examining error and warning messages and checking the search terms, date range, number of rows, missing values, and minimum and maximum values. Plotting the data and comparing repeated downloads can also reveal unexpected changes.



4.c. Repeating the Same Query
I ran the same gtrendsR query twice on September 22, 2026: first at 6:03 PM CDT and again at 6:07 PM CDT. The results were not identical. Of the 786 observations, 26 search-interest values changed, generally by only one point.
This variation shows that Google Trends results can differ because they are calculated using sampled and normalized search data. Therefore, the values should not be treated as fixed or perfectly precise measurements. Researchers should report the retrieval time, preserve the original data, acknowledge the possibility of sampling variation, and avoid drawing strong conclusions from very small numerical differences.

title: Assignment 7
text:
This collection examines comments on 2026 US midterm election coverage by NBC News, CNN, and Al Jazeera English, representing a national network, cable news, and an international broadcaster. All requests were made on November 10. “Before” and “after” primarily identify video publication periods, not separate collection waves. This retrospective design cannot reconstruct what comment sections looked like before Election Day.
I searched “US midterm election” using relevance and view-count rankings, requesting 100 videos per ordering. The publication windows were September 1–October 27 and November 4–November 10. Both rankings returned 100 rows without duplicate video IDs, while reporting approximately one million available results. Only 24 videos overlapped before the election and 29 afterward. Before the election, Al Jazeera led relevance results with 16 videos, whereas CNN led view-count results with 38. These differences demonstrate that search rankings select different coverage rather than provide a random sample.
Channel uploads supplied an alternative route. An initial 200-video request per channel reached only November 6–7; expanded 6,000-video requests reached September 1 for all three. The broad title filter also captured foreign elections and a university faculty senate. Reviewing 20 retained and 20 excluded titles motivated a narrower filter. Generic program titles could still conceal relevant coverage. Ten candidates per channel and period were randomly drawn with seed 6302 and reviewed; the first three were selected before inspecting comment counts.
The resulting 18 videos yielded 2,708 unique comments, capped at 300 per video. All collection logs recorded success. CNN reached the cap on every selected video, producing 1,800 comments; Al Jazeera contributed 275 and NBC 633. Smaller sections matched their reported totals. For capped sections, the cap explains an observed shortfall; moderation, deletion, replies, and changing counts remain possible general sources of mismatch. Missing video IDs in some returned replies were repaired using the request’s video ID before joining metadata.
A comment section is therefore a sample of visible participation under these videos, conditional on access and moderation. People who watched without commenting are absent, and prolific authors can contribute several observations. Channel differences also combine topic selection with audience responses. Consequently, neither the raw counts nor the lexical comparisons identify a causal election effect. Comparing different videos before and after the election does not hold their subjects or audiences constant.
Participation and attention were uneven. The most active 10% of identified authors produced 22.7% of comments, while the top approximately 1% of comments received 43.8% of likes. Twenty-three repeated text groups contained 60 comments. These counts do not establish automated or coordinated behavior. NBC’s after-period videos had a 33.9% reply share, compared with CNN’s 2.2%, but selected topics and collection caps limit comparisons.
The quanteda unit was one comment. URLs and mentions were removed; emoji and non-English text were retained. Context reading distinguished party references, political support, procedural discussion, grievances, and uses of “democratic” unrelated to party identity. Required phrases were compounded alongside “vote blue” and “voter fraud.” Keyness emphasized celebration and Michigan in Al Jazeera comments and interview subjects in NBC comments. CNN’s leading Arabic features originated in only three comments, with 552 occurrences. Excluding those comments shifted the ranking toward laughter, Mississippi, and ridicule, demonstrating sensitivity to concentrated repetition.
LSD2015 classified 52.0% of Al Jazeera’s after-period comments as positive, versus 23.5% before. However, AI-assisted human coding of 40 randomly selected comments agreed with the dictionary on only 57.5%, below a 70% majority-class baseline in that sample. Sarcasm, political endorsements, abbreviations, mixed evaluations, and non-English text complicate interpretation. Zero or tied dictionary scores do not demonstrate emotional neutrality. These results describe lexical classifications, not validated changes in voter sentiment.
Assignment 6’s archived Biden–Xi tweets represent platform users selected by keywords and timing; their original collection cannot be repeated through the same access. Presidential documents mentioning Xi represent institutionally produced communication selected by publication practices and a query, supporting claims about government discourse. YouTube comments instead reflect self-selected participants under selected videos, shaped by audiences, moderation, ranking, and collection time. Public reads may be repeated, but exact results will change. None of these corpora alone represents public opinion. Retained code, manifests, and aggregates document the procedure while raw YouTube data must be deleted by December 10.

Data note and reproduction
Data were collected through the YouTube Data API v3 using an API key and a quota plan. The key, raw comments, and commenter identifiers are not published. Raw API data and validation files containing comment text will be deleted by December 10, 2026.
The query was US midterm election, with 100 results requested for both relevance and viewCount orderings. Video publication windows were September 1–October 27 and November 4–10, 2026. Title-filtered uploads from Al Jazeera English, CNN, and NBC News supplied candidates. Using seed 6302, ten candidates per channel and period were sampled and reviewed; the first three were selected, with up to 300 comments collected per video. Exact settings are recorded in the manifests.
All comments were collected on November 10, so “before” and “after” refer to video publication dates. Title filters, moderation, deletion, comment ordering, language, and collection caps limit coverage. These comments do not represent all viewers or voters. Repeated API requests may return different results.
The collection script and analysis script document the workflow. Aggregate results are presented above.
